8.01.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this graft material?"
- "A **bone graft**: tissue or material used to replace missing bone."
- "Name it by source: **autograft**, allograft, DBM, synthetic or growth factor."

### By source (Handbook)
| Source | Comes from |
|---|---|
| **Autograft** | the patient's own body |
| Isograft | an identical twin |
| **Allograft** | another person, usually a cadaver |
| Xenograft | an animal |
| **Synthetic** | a factory |

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Self, twin, donor, animal, factory**

- Used for bone loss, non-union, fusion, and defects after resection

### What the examiner holds up
| Item | Looks like |
|---|---|
| **Autograft** | red, bleeding chips or block |
| **Allograft** | white bone, femoral head, sealed pack |
| **DBM** | putty or paste in a syringe |
| **Calcium sulfate** | white pellets or beads |
| **Calcium phosphate** | granules, or a paste that sets |
| **BMP** | vial plus a collagen sponge |

- DBM = demineralised bone matrix; BMP = bone morphogenetic protein
- Allografts make up about one third of grafts in the USA

- Corticocancellous autograft from the anterior iliac crest
- Femoral head allograft, bulk and morselised
- DBM putty in a 10 mL syringe
- Calcium sulfate bead mat; tricalcium phosphate granules injected
- rhBMP-2 vial with its collagen sponge

PITFALL — "is DBM a synthetic substitute?"
- DBM is made from donor bone by acid extraction
- Say → "**No. DBM is processed allograft; it keeps collagen and growth factors.**"

8.02.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how does a bone graft work?"
- "Three functions: **osteogenic** cells, **osteoinductive** signals, **osteoconductive** scaffold."
- "Only fresh autograft does all three."

### The three functions (Handbook; Rockwood)
| Function | What it is | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Osteogenic** | living cells make bone | fresh autograft, marrow |
| **Osteoinductive** | factors recruit stem cells | BMP-2, BMP-7 |
| **Osteoconductive** | scaffold for ingrowth | allograft, ceramics |

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Cells build, signals call, scaffold holds**

- Osteogenic cells need a fresh graft: processing kills them
- Heavily processed grafts are purely osteoconductive

### Which graft has which (Miller)
| Graft | Cells | Signals | Scaffold |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cancellous autograft** | excellent | good | excellent |
| Cortical autograft | fair | fair | fair |
| Allograft | none | fair | fair |
| DBM | none | fair | good |
| Ceramics | none | none | fair |
| Bone marrow | good | poor | poor |

- Structural strength: cortical autograft excellent, allograft good, cancellous poor

### Incorporation (Rockwood)
#### Steps
1) Haematoma calls in inflammatory cells
2) New vessels grow into the graft
3) Osteoclasts resorb dead graft and open channels

#### Then
4) Stem cells along the vessels make new bone
5) Remodelling matures it

#### Creeping substitution
- New bone is laid on dead trabeculae, then remodelled
- Cancellous: vascularised within days; replaced within 1 year

#### Cortical graft
- Resorbs first, so it weakens over the first **6 months**
- Strength returns at about **1 year**
- Full replacement can take **2 years**

- Creeping substitution: woven bone on dead lamellar bone
- Wrist fusion with iliac crest graft, healed at 6 months

#### Lay it at the rim
- Graft at the edge of a non-union is far stronger than central graft
- Torsional strength rises with the radius to the **3rd** power
- Bending strength rises with the radius to the **4th** power

#### Judet decortication
- Raise **2–3 mm** osteoperiosteal flakes with an osteotome
- Cover **3–4 cm** on each side of the non-union
- Treat about **two-thirds** of the circumference

### What helps the graft take
| Helps | Harms |
|---|---|
| Good blood supply | infection |
| Stable fixation | radiation |
| Large surface area | smoking, steroids |
| Mechanical loading | diabetes, malnutrition |

PITFALL — "cortical graft: strongest at six months?"
- Osteoclasts hollow it out before new bone fills in
- Say → "**No. Weakest at about 6 months; strong again by one year.**"

8.03.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "why is autograft the gold standard?"
- "It has **all three** functions and carries no disease or rejection."
- "Its price is **donor-site morbidity** and a limited amount."

### Forms
- **Cancellous**, **cortical**, **corticocancellous** (e.g. tricortical iliac block)
- **Osteochondral** plugs (mosaicplasty) for osteochondritis dissecans
- **Injectable**: bone marrow aspirate

### Cancellous vs cortical (Handbook; Campbell)
| | Cancellous | Cortical |
|---|---|---|
| Harvest | iliac crest, distal radius, proximal tibia | fibula, iliac crest, rib |
| Strength | none | structural |
| Incorporation | fast | slow |
| Use | non-union, cavities | segmental defects |

- Small cancellous sites: greater trochanter, olecranon, femoral condyle
- Leave at least **2 cm** of subchondral bone under any joint

- Tricortical iliac crest graft harvested, then fixed to the glenoid

### Vascularised or not (Rockwood)
| Defect length | Graft |
|---|---|
| Under **6 cm** | non-vascularised cortical |
| **6–12 cm** | debated |
| Over **12 cm** | vascularised |

- Also vascularised: irradiated or scarred bed, atrophic non-union
- A vascularised graft keeps up to **90%** of its osteocytes
- In cancellous autograft only about **15%** of cells survive

#### Why vascularised
- It unites like a fracture and **hypertrophies** with loading
- Fibula flap pedicle: the **peroneal** artery

- Fibula harvest: vascularised with muscle cuff; non-vascularised, bare
- Condyle-sparing vascularised fibula; double-barrel non-vascularised fibula

### Bone marrow aspirate (Rockwood)
- Taken from the iliac crest with a trocar needle
- Cells are few, so it is concentrated by centrifuge
- Small pulls: 4 mL instead of 1 mL halves cell concentration

- Bone marrow aspiration from the iliac crest, four steps

PITFALL — "a 14 cm tibial gap: non-vascularised fibula?"
- A long dead strut incorporates slowly and fractures
- Say → "**Over 12 cm, a vascularised graft; under 6 cm, non-vascularised.**"

8.04.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "where do you take a bone graft from?"
- "The **iliac crest**, anterior or posterior, is the main source."
- "Others: fibula, proximal tibia, distal radius, olecranon, and **RIA** from the femur."

### Anterior vs posterior iliac crest (Campbell; Miller)
| | Anterior | Posterior |
|---|---|---|
| Position | supine | prone |
| Amount | moderate | largest, near the SI joint |
| Nerve at risk | lateral femoral cutaneous | superior cluneal |
| Other risk | ASIS fracture | superior gluteal vessels, sciatic nerve |

- SI = sacroiliac; ASIS = anterior superior iliac spine
- Spine fusion grafts come from the **posterior third** of the crest

#### Safe-zone numbers
- Stay at least **2 cm** behind the ASIS → no fracture
- Stay within **8 cm** of the posterior superior iliac spine → cluneal nerves safe
- Most cancellous bone: the **gluteus medius pillar** above the acetabulum

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Front: two from the spine; back: eight from the spine**

- Spine infection: debride, bone graft, stabilise (Nagah)

- Crest harvest, front and back; arrow on lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
- Iliac crest incision, cancellous graft, defect filled
- Superior cluneal nerve landmarks near the posterior spine
- Posterior spinal fusion: graft laid on decorticated bone

### Iliac crest harvest — steps (Campbell)
#### Open
1) Incise along the crest, between gluteal and abdominal muscles
2) Lift the crest as a trap door, subperiosteally
3) Blunt retractor on the inner table → peritoneum and bleeding safe

#### Take
4) Cancellous: curette or gouge between the two tables
5) Tricortical block: power saw, cooled with saline
6) Do not take too much anterior crest → no deformity

#### Close
7) Repair periosteum and muscles firmly → no hernia
8) Control bleeding with packing, not bone wax

#### Saw or osteotome
- Full-thickness grafts cut with a power saw are stronger
- The saw causes less microfracture than an osteotome

### Tools
- Gouge, curette and osteotome → ch 1
- Acetabular reamers can shave graft from the crest
- Trephine: a hollow cutting tube for cores; bone mill crushes them

- Acetabular reamers used to harvest crest graft

### RIA — reamer–irrigator–aspirator (Rockwood)
- One-pass reamer that irrigates and sucks reamings into a filter

#### Use it
- Reamer **1–4 mm** larger than the narrowest canal
- Average yield about **40 mL**
- With experience, **60–80 cm³** without weakening the femur

#### How much a gap needs
- Each cm of femoral shaft defect needs **11.3 cm³** of graft
- Each cm of tibial shaft defect needs **7.1 cm³**

#### Versus the crest (AO; Campbell)
- More graft, less donor pain
- More blood loss: transfusion **44%** vs 21%
- Avoid in osteoporotic bone

- RIA system and its drawing
- Graft collected in the RIA filter

### Fibula
- Take the middle third through a lateral approach
- Keep the distal **quarter** → stable ankle
- Proximal fibula: protect the common peroneal nerve at the neck

### Other sites
- Proximal tibia: major complications in **0.5–2%**
- Distal radius: de Quervain's, superficial radial nerve, fracture

PITFALL — "extend the posterior crest incision laterally for more bone?"
- The superior cluneal nerves cross the crest from 8 cm lateral to the spine
- Say → "**No. Stay within 8 cm of the posterior superior iliac spine.**"

8.05.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this white bone graft?"
- "An **allograft**: donor bone from a bank, frozen or freeze-dried."
- "Unlimited, no donor site; but **slow** incorporation and disease risk."

### Sources
- Cadaver donors, or a femoral head taken at hip arthroplasty
- Amputee bone; now rare in Egypt, with no regulating law (Prof Abosena)

### Processing (Miller; Handbook)
| Type | Keeps | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Fresh** | cells, factors | most immunogenic; rarely used |
| **Fresh-frozen** | BMP, strength | best structural allograft |
| **Freeze-dried** | scaffold only | least immunogenic; weak |
| **Irradiated** | scaffold | weaker with higher dose |

- Fresh-frozen is stored at −70 to −80 °C
- Freeze-dried ("croutons") has the lowest viral risk

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Frozen keeps the factors; freeze-dried keeps only the scaffold**

- Femoral head allograft before and after cartilage removal
- RIA autograft, freeze-dried allograft granules, and the mix

### Forms
| Form | Use |
|---|---|
| **Particulate** chips, granules | metaphyseal cavities |
| **Cortical strut** | periprosthetic fracture, non-union |
| **Intercalary** segment | limb salvage after tumour |
| **Osteochondral** | joint surface defect |

- Also: revision arthroplasty; elderly, small children, poor-risk patients

- Circumferential cortical strut allografts on a humeral non-union
- Structural allograft thawed, then incorporated over a nail
- Distal femoral allograft fixed with a plate

### Why it is slow (Miller; Rockwood)
- Few cells, and the host's T cells react to it
- Marrow cells provoke the strongest reaction
- Vessels rarely reach beyond **5 mm** in 2 years

#### Help it
- Put autograft at the allograft–host junction
- Mixed grafts incorporate faster than allograft alone

#### Disease
- Donors are screened for HIV and hepatitis B and C

### Strut graft for fibrous dysplasia (Nagah)
- After a fracture: extended curettage + cortical strut (fibula or rib)

PITFALL — "fill fibrous dysplasia with cancellous autograft?"
- Miller: transplanted cancellous bone turns into fibrous dysplasia bone
- Say → "**Never. Use a cortical strut, best allograft fibula.**"

8.06.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this white material in a syringe?"
- "A **bone graft substitute**: DBM, or a calcium sulfate or phosphate filler."
- "They fill **contained** voids; none bridges a segmental gap alone."

### DBM (Rockwood)
- Acid extraction of allograft bone
- Keeps type I collagen and BMPs; no strength
- Forms: powder, granules, gel, putty, strips

#### Use
- Each batch comes from **one** donor, so BMP content varies
- Best as an extender mixed with autograft

### Calcium-based fillers (Rockwood; Miller)
| Filler | Resorbs in | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Calcium sulfate** | **6–12 weeks** | weakest |
| **Tricalcium phosphate** | 6–24 months | partly turns into hydroxyapatite |
| **Hydroxyapatite** | **2–5 years** | slow, brittle |
| **Calcium phosphate cement** | very slow | strongest in compression |

- All are osteoconductive only, and weak in shear
- Calcium phosphate ceramics are sintered above **1,000 °C**
- Best ingrowth with pores over **150 μm**

### Calcium sulfate (plaster of Paris)
- Pellets, beads or injectable paste
- Used as an **antibiotic carrier**; resorbs by about **8 weeks**

#### Its problem
- **Serous wound discharge** (Handbook)
- Campbell: whitish drainage without fever, cellulitis or raised white cells

- Calcium sulfate beads around a hip; beads resorbed at 2 years

### Calcium phosphate cement
- Injectable paste; hardens in minutes
- Full strength at about **4 hours**
- Strength like cancellous bone in compression

#### Uses
- Under a lifted tibial plateau, distal radius, calcaneus, proximal humerus
- Less loss of reduction than autograft

- Calcium phosphate cement injected into a bone cyst

### Hydroxyapatite and collagen
- **Coralline** hydroxyapatite: coral skeleton converted by heat and pressure
- Pores **200–500 μm**, like trabecular bone
- Collagen: bovine type I, used as a BMP carrier

PITFALL — "calcium sulfate under a tibial plateau, walk at once?"
- It loses strength in weeks as it resorbs
- Say → "**No. For early load, calcium phosphate cement is stronger.**"

8.07.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is BMP and where is it used?"
- "**Bone morphogenetic protein**: it turns stem cells into osteoblasts."
- "**BMP-2** and **BMP-7** reached clinical use; they need a carrier."

### BMP (Rockwood; Campbell)
| BMP | Approved use |
|---|---|
| **BMP-2** | open tibial fracture, spine fusion |
| **BMP-7** (OP-1) | recalcitrant tibial non-union |

- Carrier: absorbable collagen sponge
- BMP-7 has since left the market

#### Tibial non-union trial
- OP-1 healed **81%**; autograft healed **85%** at 9 months
- OP-1's gain: no donor-site pain

- Tibial non-union healed with OP-1 over 24 months

#### Risks
- Inflammation and swelling, ectopic bone
- Possible cancer risk; retrograde ejaculation after anterior lumbar fusion
- Not approved in children or pregnancy

### PRP and marrow
- **PRP**: platelet-rich plasma, spun from the patient's blood
- Platelets **300–600%** of normal; no proof it heals non-union

#### Marrow concentrate
- **BMAC**: iliac aspirate spun to raise cell numbers
- Tibial non-union healed when cells exceeded **1,000/cm³**

- PRP layer after centrifuge

PITFALL — "BMP for a child's ulnar non-union?"

8.08.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you fill a big bone gap?"
- "**Masquelet** induced membrane, **bone transport**, or a **vascularised fibula**."
- "Cancellous graft alone fails beyond about **5–6 cm**."

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Induced membrane** | cement spacer, then graft |
| **Bone transport** | Ilizarov → ch 3 |
| **Vascularised fibula** | defects over 12 cm |
| **Structural allograft** | tumour, revision |

### Masquelet technique (AO; Rockwood)
#### Stage 1
1) Debride all dead bone; stabilise
2) Fill the gap with an antibiotic **PMMA spacer** (polymethylmethacrylate)
3) A membrane forms around the spacer

#### Stage 2, at 4–8 weeks
4) Incise the membrane; slide the spacer out
5) **Keep the membrane**; pack it with cancellous autograft
6) Close the membrane; fix with nail or plate

#### Why it works
- The membrane secretes BMP-2 and growth factors, peaking at **4 weeks**
- It holds the graft and stops its resorption

#### Numbers
- Defects of **4–25 cm** treated in Masquelet's series
- Full rebuilding takes **1–2 years**
- Better in the femur than the tibia: thicker muscle cover

- Two-stage Masquelet: spacer, membrane, graft, nail
- Membrane after spacer removal; femoral defect healed with crest graft
- Beads in a 17 cm gap; then cages, RIA graft, calcium sulfate

#### Harborview
- Do not overstuff the membrane
- Bear weight when new bone is half as dense as normal

### Vascularised fibula (AO)
- It hypertrophies only slowly (see 8.3)
- Thin, so best for forearm and humerus
- Tibia: consider a double fibula

- Vascularised fibula harvested with a skin paddle

#### Prof Abosena
- Fibula risks: venous gangrene, compartment syndrome
- Membrane: no long-term tumour results; staging clashes with chemotherapy

| Recycled tumour bone | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Liquid nitrogen freezing | best: keeps BMP, strength |
| Autoclaving, boiling | worst |
| Pasteurisation | if heating is unavoidable |
| Irradiation, **20–30 Gy** | if heating is unavoidable |

- Needs at least **3** intact cortices

### Antibiotic beads and spacers (Campbell; Rockwood)
- PMMA beads strung on wire; cement → ch 10.8
- Mix **2–4 g** antibiotic per 40 g cement

#### Beads vs block
- Beads give higher early antibiotic levels than a block spacer
- Beads are hard to remove after **4 weeks**
- Calcium sulfate beads dissolve: no second operation

- PMMA bead chain; beads filling a debrided wound

PITFALL — "excise the membrane at stage two?"
- The membrane carries the blood supply and the growth factors
- Say → "**No. Open it, remove the spacer, keep it, fill it with graft.**"

8.09.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "complications of bone grafting?"
- "**Donor site**: pain, nerve injury, hernia, fracture, haematoma, infection."
- "**Graft**: failure to incorporate, infection, disease, serous discharge."

### Donor site (Rockwood)
| Complication rate | Range |
|---|---|
| Minor | **7.1–39%** |
| Major | **1.8–10%** |

#### Iliac crest
| Problem | Rate |
|---|---|
| Pain | **2–26%** |
| Infection | 0–7.5% |
| Lateral femoral cutaneous symptoms | **0–16%** |

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Pain, nerve, hernia, fracture, bleed, infect**

#### Rare but severe
- Hernia after full-thickness grafts (see 8.4, step 7)
- Arterial injury, false aneurysm, ureteral injury
- ASIS avulsion, pelvic instability, cosmetic deformity

#### RIA
- Femoral fracture or cortical perforation; blood loss (see 8.4)

- RIA perforated the anterior femoral cortex
- ASIS fracture after iliac crest harvest, on CT

### The graft
- Failure to incorporate can happen even with autograft
- Allograft: infection, non-union, late fracture
- Massive cortical grafts: insufficiency fracture in **25%**

#### Fillers
- Calcium phosphate cement can discharge too (calcium sulfate: see 8.6)

- Structural allograft non-union, later converted to arthroplasty

#### On the X-ray
- Graft resorbs and fades
- Lucent line at the host junction
- Graft fracture or broken fixation

### Contraindications (Handbook)
- Active infection in the bed
- Ischaemic or non-viable bed

PITFALL — "graft the infected non-union now?"
- Graft placed in pus dies as a sequestrum
- Say → "**Debride first, control infection, get soft-tissue cover, then graft.**"
